fixes.explanation: It's the other way around. The text says he "…cannot deliver himself…" (Isaiah 44:20). He holds the thing in his right hand and still can't ask whether it's a lie. His deluded heart has led him astray, so he can't see it for himself.

That's right, he can't. The text says he "…cannot deliver himself…" (Isaiah 44:20). The thing is right there in his right hand, and he still can't ask whether it's a lie. His deluded heart has led him astray.

Maker is the word. The LORD calls Himself the One "…who formed you from the womb…" (Isaiah 44:2). Jacob is the name He uses here for His people. He also says He is the One "…who will help you…", and I'd say that's a pretty good way to start a message.

Shepherd is a lovely word, and the Bible does use it elsewhere: "The LORD is my shepherd…" (Psalm 23:1). Here, though, the LORD calls Himself Jacob's Maker, the One who formed him from the womb. Jacob is the name He uses here for His people. I think I'd have picked Shepherd too, because I love a good sheep picture, but this verse sticks with Maker.
The text says the opposite, friend. Right after "I am the first and I am the last…" the LORD says, “…and there is no God but Me.” (Isaiah 44:6). Nothing in that sentence puts another god beside Him.

Yes, it's False. The LORD says, “I am the first and I am the last, and there is no God but Me.” (Isaiah 44:6). Right after calling Himself the first and the last, He says there is no God but Him. No other god is named beside Him in that line.

I see why a fear-not speech might lead to soldiers. But the LORD says something different: “You are My witnesses!” (Isaiah 44:8). A witness is someone who says what's true about what the LORD has told them, friend.
That's right. The LORD says, “There is no other Rock; I know not one.” (Isaiah 44:8). He doesn't just say there's no other. He adds that He knows not one.
The text says their witnesses "…fail to see or comprehend, so they are put to shame." (Isaiah 44:9). Seeing and understanding are what's missing. Those are the two things the verse names.

Stand or walk is a fair guess for something a witness might do. But in this verse, the text is talking about the witnesses. They "…fail to see or comprehend, so they are put to shame." (Isaiah 44:9). It's about what they can see and understand, not about their legs.

Wealthy would be a nice reward for all that hammering. But the text says something different. “Yet he grows hungry and loses his strength; he fails to drink water and grows faint.” (Isaiah 44:12). The verse is about his strength, not his money.

A bull is a fair guess, but this verse says something else. The woodworker "…fashions it in the likeness of man, like man in all his glory, that it may dwell in a shrine." (Isaiah 44:13). This idol is shaped like a person.

The text says, “…He has shut their eyes so they cannot see and closed their minds so they cannot understand.” (Isaiah 44:18). That's the reason this verse gives for why they don't see how foolish it is. It's a hard verse, and I think it's worth sitting with.

The text says, “He feeds on ashes.” (Isaiah 44:20). Earlier, he burned half of the wood to roast meat and eat (Isaiah 44:16). This verse then says he feeds on ashes, and ashes won't fill anybody, friend.
Smoke fits the fire scene, I'll give you that. But the text says, “He feeds on ashes.” (Isaiah 44:20). So the word is ashes, not smoke.

The text says, “For the LORD has redeemed Jacob, and revealed His glory in Israel.” (Isaiah 44:23). That's the reason for the song. The heavens are told to sing for joy, the depths of the earth to shout aloud, and the mountains, forests and trees to break forth in song. That's a lot of voices, and I think it's worth listening.
